WMT.rationale: Walmart is a fundamentally sound business with durable competitive advantages, but the current valuation is extremely stretched and leaves no margin of safety. The stock trades at 54.5x trailing P/E (vs. 33x a year ago), 11.8x P/B (vs. 8.4x a year ago), and an earnings yield of just 1.8% — all at or near the top of of the3 the window. The.............0   ..%, margin,,, andThe, and.28% operating margin of 4.3% of sales, and operating income growth of 6-8% YoY, but QoQ operating income declined 14.9% and operating cash flow fell 29.7%. The TTM data is incomplete due to fiscal calendar gaps, but the available evidence does not support paying a premium this extreme. A DCF model cited in the Wedbush research report values the stock at $83, implying >337% downside from the current $132 price. The market appears to be capitalizing a 'tech-powered flywheel' narrative — advertising, AI, automation — well ahead of realized earnings. While Walmart Connect grew 46% in FY26 and e-commerce crossed $100B, consolidated operating margin remains a modest 4.2% and actually declined 13bps YoY. The business is a best-in-class retailer, not a high-margin technology company, yet it is priced as one. Grocery market share is also slipping (19.9% in 2026 vs. 20.4% in 2024 per Numerator). There is no near-term fundamental catalyst to justify a re-rating higher; Q1 FY27 results on May 21 come with conservative guidance (3.5-4.5% revenue growth, $2.75-2.85 EPS vs. Street's $2.97), and the macro backdrop includes rising oil prices ($108/bbl WTI), elevated 10Y yields (4.4%), and tariff uncertainty. The risk/reward is heavily skewed to the downside at this valuation.
